o: Transmits the glossopharyngeal nerve through its posterior part

IX passes through the anterior (medial) part, with the inferior petrosal sinus.
X and XI pass through the middle part.
Transmits the sigmoid sinus through its anterior part

The sigmoid sinus passes through the posterior (lateral) part, becoming the internal jugular vein.
This is the largest part of the foramen.
Transmits the hypoglossal nerve

XII leaves through the hypoglossal canal, above the condyle.
It joins the vagus just outside the skull.
Transmits the inferior petrosal sinus through its anterior part

The inferior petrosal sinus passes through the anterior part to join the internal jugular vein.
IX lies alongside it.
Transmits the glossopharyngeal nerve

IX leaves through the jugular foramen.
The meatus transmits VII, nervus intermedius and VIII.
Transmits the labyrinthine artery

The labyrinthine artery, usually from AICA, enters the meatus to the inner ear.
It is an end artery.
Has the facial nerve in the lower part of its fundus

The facial nerve lies in the upper anterior part of the fundus.
The cochlear nerve is below it, the vestibular nerves behind.
Transmits the facial nerve, nervus intermedius and vestibulocochlear nerve

These pass from the cerebellopontine angle into the meatus together.
An acoustic neuroma here can compress VII as well as VIII.
Transmits the mandibular nerve

The mandibular nerve passes through it into the infratemporal fossa.
It divides about 4–5 mm below. (Last's p. 633)
Transmits the middle meningeal artery

The middle meningeal artery enters through the foramen spinosum, just behind and lateral.
The accessory meningeal artery uses the foramen ovale.
Lies in the petrous temporal bone

It lies in the greater wing of the sphenoid.
The foramen spinosum is also in the greater wing.
Transmits the greater petrosal nerve

The greater petrosal runs to the foramen lacerum.
The lesser petrosal often passes through the foramen ovale (or a small canal near it).
Is traversed vertically from below by the internal carotid artery

The artery enters the cranium across the upper end of the foramen from the carotid canal.
It does not pass up through it from below.
Is open in life

It is closed below by fibrocartilage in life.
Only small structures pierce it.
Transmits the maxillary nerve

The maxillary nerve leaves through the foramen rotundum.
The foramen lacerum lies further back, at the petrous apex.
Is where the greater and deep petrosal nerves join

They join at the foramen lacerum to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal.
That nerve runs forward to the pterygopalatine ganglion.
Is where frontal, parietal, sphenoid and temporal bones meet

It is an H-shaped junction on the side of the skull.
It is the thinnest part of the vault.
Lies about 3 cm above the midpoint of the zygomatic arch

It is also about 3 cm behind the frontozygomatic suture.
This is the burr-hole site for the frontal branch. (Last's p. 562)
Overlies the frontal branch of the middle meningeal artery

The frontal branch runs deep to the pterion, often in a bony canal.
A blow here can tear it and cause an extradural haematoma.
Overlies the transverse sinus

The transverse sinus lies at the back of the skull, along the attached margin of the tentorium.
The pterion overlies the stem of the lateral sulcus.
Is a branch of the second part of the maxillary artery

It arises from the first part, before lateral pterygoid.
First- and third-part branches go through bony foramina. (Last's p. 459)
Enters the skull through the foramen spinosum

It enters through the foramen spinosum with the nervus spinosus.
It then grooves the squamous temporal bone.
Supplies the cerebral cortex

It supplies the dura and the bone of the vault, not the brain.
The brain gets its blood from the internal carotid and vertebral systems.
Bleeds into the extradural space when torn

The artery lies between dura and bone, so tearing it strips the dura off.
This forms an extradural haematoma, classically after a pterion fracture.
Is attached anteriorly to the crista galli

The falx is attached in front to the crista galli.
Behind, it fuses with the tentorium.
Has the straight sinus in its lower free margin

The inferior sagittal sinus runs in the lower free margin.
The straight sinus lies along the junction of falx and tentorium.
Is attached anteriorly to the tentorium cerebelli

It joins the tentorium at the back, along the straight sinus.
The front end is free above the corpus callosum.
Separates the two cerebellar hemispheres

That is the falx cerebelli, a small fold below the tentorium.
The falx cerebri lies between the cerebral hemispheres.
Has its free margin attached to the posterior clinoid processes

The free margin runs forward to the anterior clinoid processes.
The attached margin ends at the posterior clinoid processes.
Has the transverse sinus in its free margin

The transverse sinus is in the attached margin, on the occipital bone.
The free margin bounds the tentorial notch.
Is supplied by upper cervical nerves

It is supplied by tentorial branches of the ophthalmic nerve.
Dura below it is supplied by upper cervical nerves and the vagus.
Bounds the tentorial notch through which the midbrain passes

The free margin forms the notch around the midbrain.
Herniation of the uncus through the notch compresses III and the midbrain.
Receives the superior cerebral veins

They open into it, often against the flow, after crossing the subdural space.
Tearing these bridging veins causes subdural haematoma.
Has arachnoid granulations projecting into its lateral lacunae

CSF passes back into the blood through the granulations.
They indent the vault bone with age.
Usually drains into the right transverse sinus

At the confluence it usually turns right, while the straight sinus turns left.
So the right sigmoid sinus and internal jugular are usually larger.
Communicates with scalp veins through emissary veins

The parietal emissary veins link it to scalp veins.
Scalp infection can spread inward this way.
Grooves the occipital bone only

It grooves the mastoid part of the temporal bone, then the occipital bone.
It is close to the mastoid antrum.
Drains into the inferior petrosal sinus

It continues through the jugular foramen as the internal jugular vein.
The inferior petrosal sinus joins the vein outside the skull.
Is a continuation of the straight sinus

It continues from the transverse sinus.
The straight sinus drains into the confluence, usually turning left.
Becomes the internal jugular vein at the jugular foramen

It passes through the posterior part of the foramen.
The superior bulb of the vein lies just below.
Has the hypoglossal canal above the jugular tubercle

The canal lies below the jugular tubercle, above the occipital condyle.
The tubercle lies between hypoglossal canal and jugular foramen.
Has the internal occipital crest for the falx cerebelli

The falx cerebelli is attached to the internal occipital crest.
The occipital sinus runs in its attached margin.
Has a clivus formed by the occipital bone alone

The clivus is formed by basisphenoid and basiocciput.
Their junction is about 2.5 cm in front of the foramen magnum. (Last's p. 649)
Has the transverse sinus groove along the attached margin of the tentorium

The groove marks where the tentorium is attached to the occipital bone.
It continues as the sigmoid groove.
Has the cribriform plate transmitting olfactory filaments

About 20 filaments on each side pass through the cribriform plate.
A fracture here can give anosmia and CSF rhinorrhoea. (Last's p. 568)
Has a floor formed mainly by the frontal sinus

The floor is mainly the orbital plates of the frontal bone, with the cribriform plate in the middle.
The frontal sinus lies in front of it, at varying size.
Has its posterior border formed by the lesser wings bearing the posterior clinoid processes

The lesser wings end medially as the anterior clinoid processes.
The posterior clinoid processes are on the dorsum sellae.
Lets the anterior ethmoidal nerve leave through the optic canal

The anterior ethmoidal nerve passes through its own foramen into the fossa and then into the nose.
The optic canal transmits the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery.
The sphenoidal sinus lies below

The sinus lies below and in front, allowing transsphenoidal surgery.
Its size varies a lot.
The cavernous sinuses lie on each side

Each cavernous sinus lies lateral, containing the internal carotid and VI.
III, IV, V1 and V2 lie in its lateral wall.
The optic chiasma lies above

The chiasma lies above the diaphragma sellae, in front of the stalk.
So a tumour growing up compresses it, giving bitemporal hemianopia.
The basilar artery lies directly in front of it

The basilar artery lies behind the dorsum sellae, on the clivus.
In front is the tuberculum sellae.
Transmits the ophthalmic vein

Ophthalmic veins go through the superior orbital fissure.
The optic canal transmits the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery.
Lies between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid

It passes through the lesser wing and body.
The superior orbital fissure lies between greater and lesser wings.
Contains an optic nerve with no meningeal sheath

The nerve carries dura, arachnoid and pia through the canal.
The subarachnoid space extends to the back of the eye.
Transmits the ophthalmic artery below the optic nerve

The artery lies below and lateral to the nerve in the canal.
It then crosses the nerve in the orbit.
Transmits the frontal nerve

The frontal nerve passes through the superior orbital fissure.
It runs forward on levator palpebrae.
Transmits the zygomatic nerve

The zygomatic nerve enters the orbit through it.
It carries the lacrimal secretomotor fibres.
Connects the orbit with the middle cranial fossa

It connects the orbit with the pterygopalatine and infratemporal fossae.
The superior orbital fissure connects with the middle cranial fossa.
Transmits the infraorbital nerve and vessels

The maxillary nerve enters as the infraorbital nerve, deviating laterally about 1 cm.
It then runs in the infraorbital groove. (Last's p. 511)

questions.s: The pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the:
o: Middle cranial fossa through the foramen rotundum

The maxillary nerve enters through the foramen rotundum.
It is the main content of the fossa.
Nasal cavity through the sphenopalatine foramen

Nasal nerves and the sphenopalatine artery pass through it.
This is the main artery of the nose.
Infratemporal fossa through the pterygomaxillary fissure

The maxillary artery enters through this fissure.
It is the third part of the artery.
Palate through the greater palatine canal

Greater and lesser palatine nerves and vessels go down this canal.
They reach the hard and soft palate.
The mastoid emissary vein joins the sigmoid sinus to the posterior auricular vein

It passes through the mastoid foramen.
Mastoid infection can spread along it to the sinus.
Diploic veins have valves

Diploic veins, like all cranial veins, have no valves.
They lie in channels in the diploe.
Emissary veins carry blood only out of the skull

Being valveless, they can carry blood either way.
So infection can spread from the scalp into the sinuses.
The parietal emissary vein passes through the foramen magnum

It passes through the parietal foramen, near the sagittal suture.
It joins the superior sagittal sinus to scalp veins.
The mastoid antrum lies about 5 mm deep to the suprameatal triangle

The antrum lies about 15 mm deep to it in the adult.
It is much shallower in the child. (Last's p. 650)
The mastoid process is present at birth

The mastoid process develops after birth, in the second year, as the sternocleidomastoid pulls.
So the facial nerve is very superficial in the newborn.
The tegmen tympani separates the middle ear from the posterior cranial fossa

The tegmen tympani separates the middle ear from the middle cranial fossa.
Middle-ear infection can spread up through it to the temporal lobe.
The suprameatal triangle is the surface marking of the mastoid antrum

The triangle lies behind and above the external acoustic meatus.
It is the surgical approach to the antrum.
